lessons.title: Before the snap
lessons.objective: You can tell offside from false start.

payload.prompt: A defender is across the line when the ball is snapped.

scene.alt: Overhead view of the line of scrimmage. A defender's helmet is past the ball's line at the snap.

explanation.correct: A defender cannot be in the neutral zone when the ball is snapped. It is five yards, and the offense can decline the flag if the play went well.
explanation.incorrect: The line of scrimmage is the ball's tip. A defender past it at the snap is offside for five yards.

payload.prompt: An offensive lineman tenses up but does not move at all.

scene.alt: Overhead view of the line. An offensive lineman is at the line of scrimmage looking tense.

explanation.correct: False start needs actual movement that looks like the start of the play. Tensing up without moving is legal.
explanation.incorrect: A false start is real movement before the snap, like a lineman rocking forward or a back shifting. Staying still, however tense, is fine.
explanation.sayThisLine: He tensed up but did not move, so it is legal.

payload.prompt: The play clock hits zero and the offense has not snapped.

scene.alt: A scoreboard showing the play clock at zero with the offense lined up but not moving.

explanation.correct: When the play clock expires, it is delay of game on the offense: five yards, and the down is replayed.
explanation.incorrect: The offense must snap before the play clock runs out. Delay of game costs five yards and the down is replayed.
explanation.sayThisLine: Delay of game, they ran out of time.

payload.prompt: Match the pre-snap flag to what triggered it.

pairs.definition: A defender is across the line of scrimmage when the ball is snapped.
An offensive player moves before the snap.
The offense fails to snap before the play clock runs out.

explanation.summary: Offside is the defense across the line. False start is the offense moving. Delay of game is running out the clock.
explanation.sayThisLine: False start again? Their tackle is jumpy.

lessons.title: Holding
lessons.objective: You can explain why holding is called so often and what it costs.

payload.prompt: How many yards is a holding penalty on offense?

options.text: Five yards
Ten yards
Fifteen yards

explanation.correct: Ten yards on the offense. On defense it is only five yards but the offense gets an automatic first down.
explanation.incorrect: Offensive holding is ten yards from the line of scrimmage. Defensive holding is less (five yards) but gives a free first down.

payload.prompt: Offensive tackle grabs a defender's jersey to create space.

scene.alt: A football play with an offensive lineman holding a defensive player's uniform.

explanation.correct: Grabbing the jersey is illegal holding. Blockers can use their hands but not grab and hang on.
explanation.incorrect: Grabbing is holding. Blockers can use their hands but must release quickly and not grab fabric or pads.

payload.prompt: Why does a blocker's hand on a defender not always draw a flag?

options.text: Blockers may use their hands inside the frame; holding is grabbing or hooking
Hands are never allowed when blocking
Holding is not a penalty in modern football

explanation.correct: Blockers can push with open hands against a defender's chest. It becomes holding when the blocker grabs, hooks or pulls to restrict him.
explanation.incorrect: Holding is a real penalty, but blocking with hands is part of the game. The flag comes when a blocker grabs or pulls a defender to stop him.

payload.prompt: Offense held on a first-down catch. Accept or decline?

situation.narrative: You are the defense. The offense completed a pass for a first down, but a holding flag is down on the offense.

facts.label: If accepted
facts.value: Replay second down, 18 yards to go

options.label: Accept the penalty
options.consequence: The catch is erased. The offense is moved back ten yards and faces second and 18.
considerations: The offense loses the first down
Second and 18 is a hard spot
Ten yards is worth more than this play

options.label: Decline and keep the result
options.consequence: The offense keeps its first down, so the flag does nothing for you.
considerations: The offense keeps the ball moving
You give up the chance to set them back
A first down beats second and 18

payload.expertNote: The team that did not foul picks the better option. Here the penalty is far worse for the offense than the gain, so you accept. You would decline if the play gained much less than the penalty, like a long run.

lessons.title: Pass interference
lessons.objective: You can explain why pass interference is such a big deal.

payload.prompt: In the NFL, pass interference is a spot foul. What does that mean?

options.text: The penalty is enforced where the foul happened
The penalty is enforced at midfield
The offense gets an automatic touchdown

explanation.correct: A spot foul means the ball is placed at the spot of the foul. If interference happens at the opponent's 10-yard line, the ball goes to the 10.
explanation.incorrect: Spot foul means the ball is placed where the foul occurred. This can give the offense huge gains and is why fans argue about it.

payload.prompt: Defender contacts receiver before the ball arrives.

situation.narrative: The receiver is running a route and the defender is running with him. The defender initiates contact by pushing. The ball is still five yards away.

options.label: Pass interference
options.consequence: Contact that hinders a catchable ball before it arrives is pass interference. The offense gets the ball at the spot of the foul.
considerations: Contact happened before the ball arrived

options.label: Incidental contact, no flag
options.consequence: Pushing a receiver who is running to a catchable ball is not incidental. It should be flagged.

payload.expertNote: Pass interference is contact that hinders a receiver's chance to catch a catchable ball in the air. When both players are playing the ball, normal contact is allowed.

payload.prompt: Defender and receiver both jump. Defender lands on the receiver.

scene.alt: A football play with a defender and receiver competing for a ball in the air, defender on top after landing.

explanation.correct: Once the ball is in the air, both players can compete. Landing on each other after jumping is legal incidental contact.
explanation.incorrect: After the ball is in flight, it is a catch battle, not interference. Incidental contact during the jump and landing is allowed.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: That should have been pass interference. He was all over him.

payload.question: What is he saying?

options.text: The defender held or grabbed the receiver before the ball arrived
The receiver caught the ball illegally
The defense committed a penalty and gave up a touchdown
Contact after the throw arrived was too physical

payload.translation: The defender was using his hands or body to prevent the receiver from running his route or catching the ball before the pass arrived.

followUps.line: Did the ball get there, or was the contact before it?
followUps.why: Timing matters: before the ball arrives is interference, after is legal.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, ask: 'Before the ball got there or after?' That tells you if it is interference.

lessons.title: Protecting players
lessons.objective: You can name the hits the league bans and why.

payload.prompt: Match the illegal hit to what the rule protects.

pairs.definition: A defender hits or drives the quarterback down after the ball is released. Fifteen yards.
A tackle where the defender uses hip and leg drive on the ball carrier's legs, banned since 2024. Fifteen yards.
College only: forcible contact to the head or neck area. Ejection when confirmed.

explanation.summary: Roughing protects the quarterback at the moment of release. Hip-drop bans a specific tackle to reduce leg injuries. Targeting bans hits to the head in college.
explanation.sayThisLine: That is roughing the passer, fifteen yards.

payload.prompt: Defensive end hits the quarterback a full step after he throws.

scene.alt: A defensive lineman hitting the quarterback a moment after the ball has left his hand.

explanation.correct: That is roughing the passer. Once the ball is gone, a defender has to pull up. It costs fifteen yards and gives the offense a first down.
explanation.incorrect: A late hit on a passer who has already thrown is roughing. A hit right as he throws can be legal, but a step late is not.

payload.prompt: Why did the NFL ban the hip-drop tackle in 2024?

options.text: It caused too many leg and knee injuries
It was unpopular with fans
Running backs complained it was unfair

explanation.correct: The hip-drop uses leverage on a player's legs, risking serious injury. The ban prioritizes safety over an effective tackle technique.
explanation.incorrect: The ban addresses injury risk. Hip-drop tackles target the legs and can cause ACL and other damage, so the league removed the technique.

statement.speaker: Announcer
statement.text: That is targeting. They are reviewing it for an ejection.

payload.question: What did the player do?

options.text: Made a forcible hit to the head or neck of a defenseless player
Grabbed a receiver's jersey
Hit the quarterback after the ball left his hands
Missed a tackle and fell down

payload.translation: The defender hit an opponent in the head or neck area with force and the opponent was vulnerable. This is college football.

followUps.line: Is targeting in the NFL too?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know it is a college-specific rule.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Targeting is college football only. The NFL uses roughing and other flags instead.

lessons.title: Grounding and eligibility
lessons.objective: You can spot intentional grounding and illegal formation.

payload.prompt: QB under pressure throws the ball away with no receiver within 10 yards.

scene.alt: A football play with the quarterback throwing to an area with no receivers nearby.

explanation.correct: A pass has to have a realistic target, unless the quarterback has left the tackle box and gets the ball to the line of scrimmage. Throwing it at no one to avoid a sack is grounding: a loss of down and yardage.
explanation.incorrect: Throwing the ball away with no eligible receiver nearby is grounding. The quarterback has to target a receiver or be outside the tackle box.

payload.prompt: Number 73, a tackle, catches a forward pass. He did not report as eligible.

scene.alt: A football formation with a large offensive lineman catching a forward pass.

explanation.correct: Jersey number 73 is an ineligible lineman. Only backs, receivers and tight ends aligned as receivers may catch passes.
explanation.incorrect: Linemen (numbers 50-79) are ineligible unless they report to the referee before the play. Number 73 cannot catch a pass.

payload.prompt: Match the rule to what it protects or defines.

pairs.definition: Quarterback throws the ball away with no eligible receiver nearby to escape pressure.
The offense does not have seven players on the line of scrimmage at the snap.
A player allowed to catch a forward pass, identified by position and number: backs, receivers and tight ends.

explanation.summary: Grounding is a pass thrown away. Illegal formation is missing a lineman. Eligible receivers are the only ones who can legally catch.
explanation.sayThisLine: That is grounding, no one was near it.

statement.speaker: Official
statement.text: Illegal formation, only six on the line.

payload.question: What went wrong?

options.text: The offense did not have seven players aligned on the line of scrimmage
A receiver ran an illegal route
The defense was too close to the line
The quarterback was not deep enough

payload.translation: The offense needs at least seven players with their hand or foot on or near the line of scrimmage at the snap.

followUps.line: Which players count as being on the line?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know it is any position, not just linemen.

lessons.title: What is a catch?
lessons.objective: You can explain the catch rule, and why nobody agrees.

payload.prompt: In the NFL, how many feet must a receiver have in bounds for a catch?

options.text: One foot
Two feet
Any body part

explanation.correct: NFL: two feet (or another body part like a knee or buttocks). College: one foot is enough, which is a key difference between the two games.
explanation.incorrect: The NFL requires two feet inbounds with control and a football move. College is one foot, and that confusion frustrates fans.

payload.prompt: Receiver catches ball and immediately trips out of bounds.

situation.narrative: A receiver has both feet in bounds, catches the ball and takes one step before tripping and going out of bounds.

facts.label: Movement
facts.value: Forward progress stopped by going out

options.label: It is a catch
options.consequence: Two feet and control plus a football move (the step). The catch is complete.
considerations: One step is a football move

options.label: Incomplete pass
options.consequence: He has all three elements: feet, control and a move. It is caught.

payload.expertNote: A catch needs control, two feet (or another body part) down and time to become a runner, which a step shows. Once he has that, tripping afterward does not undo the catch.

payload.prompt: NFL: receiver gets one foot down inbounds, steps out of bounds. Catch?

scene.alt: Overhead of the sideline. A receiver has one foot inside the line, next step lands outside.

explanation.correct: The NFL needs two feet inbounds with control. One foot is not enough. College is one foot, which confuses everyone.
explanation.incorrect: Two feet in bounds is required in the NFL. One foot counts only in college football.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: How is that not a catch? He had both hands on it and two feet down, then it popped out when he hit the ground!

payload.question: What is she missing?

options.text: A catch also needs control that holds up, including when he goes to the ground
Catches require three feet on the ground
The ball was moving too fast
Catches only happen in the end zone

payload.translation: Hands and feet start a catch, but the receiver must keep control through the whole process, including hitting the ground, and show time to become a runner.

followUps.why: Shows you understand the third element of the catch.

followUps.line: Is the catch rule different in college?
followUps.why: Tests if you know college uses one foot instead of two.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, ask whether he kept control of the ball all the way to the ground. The rule is about control, not just touching it.

lessons.title: Flags, replay and challenges
lessons.objective: You can say what can be reviewed and who decides.

payload.prompt: Put the review process in order after a scoring play.

items.text: Touchdown or field goal is scored
Official in the booth reviews video
items.why: The command center has all the angles.

items.text: Official checks with the on-field crew

items.why: The on-field ref makes the final call.

explanation.correct: Scoring plays are automatically reviewed in the booth. The official in the booth advises the on-field referee, who makes the call.
explanation.incorrect: Automatic review of scoring plays goes to the booth. The on-field referee makes the final decision after consulting the booth.

payload.prompt: Coach has one timeout. Can he challenge a holding call?

scene.alt: A coach on the sideline holding a red flag, a referee nearby with a holding marker.

choices.label: No, only plays can be challenged

explanation.correct: Penalty flags cannot be challenged. Coaches challenge things like a catch or a fumble, while scoring plays and turnovers are reviewed automatically.
explanation.incorrect: A coach can challenge some plays, like a catch or a fumble, but not a penalty call. The referee's flag stands.

payload.prompt: Which play can a coach challenge?

options.text: Was it a catch or incomplete pass?
Was it pass interference?
Was it holding on the line?

explanation.correct: A catch or incomplete call can be challenged. Penalty flags like pass interference and holding cannot be challenged.
explanation.incorrect: Coaches can challenge plays like catches and fumbles, but not penalty calls. Once the flag is thrown, it stands.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: I am throwing the red flag! That was forward progress stopped!

payload.question: Is that challengeable?

options.text: No, forward progress is the referee's judgment and cannot be challenged
Yes, always throw the flag and let the booth decide
Yes, but only if it is during a timeout
Throw the flag on any play with a whistle

payload.translation: Where a runner's forward progress ends is a judgment call by the officials, so it is not reviewable. A failed challenge costs a timeout.

followUps.why: Tests whether you know catch, fumble and turnover calls are reviewable.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, remember that penalties and judgment calls like forward progress are not challengeable, while catches and fumbles are.

lessons.title: Speaking referee
lessons.objective: You can decode a referee announcement.

payload.prompt: Listen to the referee. What is the penalty?

audio.description: A referee's voice: 'Offside, defense, number 72. Five-yard penalty. Repeat second down.'

options.text: Offside, defense
Holding, offense
False start, offense

explanation.correct: Offside on the defense: five yards against them, and the down is replayed.
explanation.incorrect: Listen for the penalty name and the team. The ref said 'offside, defense,' number 72.

payload.prompt: Decode the referee's call.

audio.description: Referee: 'Holding, offense, number 65. Ten-yard penalty. Repeat second down.'

options.text: Holding, offense, 10 yards
options.explanation: Offensive holding is ten yards from the line of scrimmage.

options.text: Holding, defense, 5 yards
options.explanation: Defensive holding is five yards with a first down, not ten.

options.text: False start, offense, 5 yards
options.explanation: False start is five yards, not ten.

explanation.correct: Holding on the offense is ten yards. The ref said 'holding, offense, ten-yard penalty.'
explanation.incorrect: Listen for 'holding' and which team. Offensive holding is ten yards; defensive is five with a free first down.

payload.prompt: Match what the referee says to the penalty.

pairs.definition: Defender was across the line at the snap. Five yards against the defense.
Illegal grabbing. Ten yards on offense, five yards on defense with a first down.
Illegal contact that hinders a catchable pass. Spot foul in the NFL.

explanation.summary: Offside is five yards for the defense. Holding is ten (offense) or five (defense). Pass interference is a spot foul.
explanation.sayThisLine: Holding on the offense, ten yards.

statement.speaker: Official
statement.text: Holding, offense, number 71. Ten-yard penalty. Repeat second down.

payload.question: What does this mean?

options.text: The offense moves back ten yards and plays second down again
The offense gets an automatic first down
The defense declined the penalty
The down counts as a turnover

payload.translation: The offense was flagged for holding, moves back ten yards and repeats the same down. The defense chose to accept the penalty, since the team that did not foul decides.

followUps.line: When would the defense decline a penalty?
followUps.why: Shows you know the team that did not foul picks the better result for itself.
